I have a brick home built in 1930 that the previous owner fucked up and it still passed inspection.

So, I noticed my son's bedroom (back of the house) was starting to sag a little last year. The brick on the front porch (opposite corner of the home) was starting to separate. I called a foundation repair company, and I was told the foundation was pretty much perfect for such an older home. Then, this: the contractors asked why the main support beam was cut up - I had no idea.

Apparently, after talking to my neighbor, the last owners cut a 4" deep by 2' wide section of the main support beam to fit an upright freezer in the basement. They wrapped this section in aluminum foil (???) and put two tiny steel posts beneath it.

My neighbor said all I have to do is jack up the beam under my son's bedroom until it's near level again and replace the 2 2x4 posts there. I was planning on starting this project today, but I'm a little overwhelmed. The contractors said I had to replace the entire beam, install several lally columns and spend thousands.

So, here's my plan: find the lowest point on the beam (I'm guessing my son's room but could be where the idiots cut out the damned beam). Place a jack post there and slowly, over several months, raise the area, then add lally columns once level enough. The jack post I bought holds up to 18k lbs, so I was thinking of renting shoring posts or just using the leftover 4x4's from a fencing project to use as temporary added support with the jack post.

Here are the symptoms of the issue: son's bedroom door frame is slowly falling away from the wall, max 3/4" opening now. Directly beneath his door is where the old wood posts are. I can feel the main support beam raise up pretty much where the cutout part is on the floor above. Floors are starting to squeak from the cutout area to where my son's room is, and I don't want to repair that until the house is more level.

Is this a terribly stupid and dangerous idea?

I'm no carpenter so take my advice with a grain of salt. I had a similar problem with my bathroom. It's an addition to the house so the floor joists and main support beam in the center of the house we're all notched out for the waste line. After repositioning the waste line I raised the sagging beam like you're planning to do and when it was level end to end I attached pressure treated 2x8s on both sides of it with bolts running through. This ran end to end and the new boards rested on the foundation walls. Basically adding a new beam without removing the old one.

hey there, i'm an engineer who works in this field. your repair strategy sounds valid. one column at each end of the notch should be enough to restore the building to its original strength, as long as you dont mind the addition of two new columns into the basement below. the columns could be wood, but im not going to try to guess a size because i don't know how much of the house this particular beam is carrying. They should each have one of those metal bases that holds the post above any water that might collect. Make sure you place a decent footing under each of your columns or you'll have the same issue again in a few more years when those columns start sinking. Also, you probably don't need to spend months jacking it. A week or two is probably slow enough. you should also expect to have to repair cracks in the sheetrock as you jack the house up.

There is an additional issue to consider though: this kind of repair probably requires a permit, and the city or county may require you to have a licensed engineer sign off on it. It is probably in your best interest anyway to have a licensed structural engineer come look at the beam and give you an assessment of the effectiveness of the repair. Depending on where you live, you might be able to get away without this step, but you do so at your own risk.
